# Experiments versus corpora {#sec-strategies} ::: {.callout-important} ## AI-generated — not for publication The code and prose in this book were written by an AI agent (Claude Code) under human direction. They have not been verified line by line and must not be published or cited as they stand. ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Preliminary and unvetted These are exploratory analyses. The models are deliberately minimal, and statements about the published literature come from memory or from an unverified literature pass. Check before relying on any of it. ::: ::: {#setup-strategies .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} %run _setup.py import json R = json.load(open("results/empirical.json")) %matplotlib inline ``` ::: ## The question How could the functional form of the threshold be tested? There are two routes. An experiment controls $N$ and $e$ exactly but is confined to small classes and to children. Corpus data cover two orders of magnitude in $N$ for free, because a child's vocabulary grows, but $N$ and $e$ have to be estimated and productivity has to be measured indirectly. This chapter sets out what each route would take and where each one currently fails. Figures of our own analyses are drawn from aggregates of two public datasets, Wordbank (parent report) and CHILDES (transcripts). ## The experimental route ### The design the question calls for The signature of a threshold that depends on $N$ is a reversal: a higher proportion of exceptions tolerated in a small class than is rejected in a large one. No fixed cutoff can produce that. Two cells carry the test, and two more show that each class size can go either way. | Cell | $N$ | Exceptions | Share | $N/\ln N$ | Fixed 40% | Majority | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Key 1 | 9 | 4 | 44% | productive | not | productive | | Key 2 | 24 | 9 | 38% | not (threshold 7.6) | productive | productive | | Control | 9 | 6 | 67% | not | not | not | | Control | 24 | 5 | 21% | productive | productive | productive | Everything else must be held constant across cells: laboratory, age, task, kind of exception, tokens per item. The existing evidence for a reversal compares studies that differ in all of these (@sec-evidence). ### Why it is hard - **It has to be run with children.** Adults match frequencies in every study, so they cannot show the effect. - **Twenty-four items is a lot for a six-year-old.** @schuler2016 used 72 sentences for 9 nouns. Matching exposure per noun means about 190 sentences, probably over several sessions. - **What matters is the lexicon the child actually learned.** A child who fails to learn some exceptions has a smaller effective $e$ than the design intended. Each child's learned $N$ and $e$ need to be measured after training and used in the analysis. - **Sample size.** Children's responses in @schuler2016 were close to all-or-none. If 85% of children are categorical in a cell predicted productive and 15% in a cell predicted not, about 8 per cell would do. With 70% against 30%, it is about 23 per cell, so roughly 90 children. Getting clean quantitative data from young children in a task this long is a serious obstacle. That motivates the corpus route. ## The corpus route ### Development as a sweep over $N$ For a given rule, the number of exceptions a child knows is a function of vocabulary size, $e(N)$. Each candidate threshold predicts the vocabulary size at which the rule should become productive: where $e(N)$ first falls below $N/\ln N$, or where $e(N)/N$ first falls below a fixed share. ::: {#cell-fig-map .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} m = R["irregular_map"] k = np.array(m["all_k"]); irr = np.array(m["all_irregular"]) fig, ax = plt.subplots() ax.plot(k, irr, lw=1.6, label="irregular verbs among the top k") ax.plot(k[1:], k[1:] / np.log(k[1:]), "k--", lw=1, label="k / ln k") ax.plot(k, 0.3 * k, ":", color="C1", label="30% of k") ax.plot(k, 0.5 * k, ":", color="C2", label="50% of k") ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_ylim(3, 300); ax.set_xlim(8, 1500) ax.set_xlabel("k (verbs, by input frequency)"); ax.set_ylabel("count"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![English verbs in child-directed speech, ranked by frequency: number of irregulars among the top k, against three thresholds. If verbs were learned in frequency order, the rule would become productive where the curve drops below a threshold.](08-strategies_files/figure-html/fig-map-output-1.png){#fig-map} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-map .cell tbl-cap='Irregular verbs among the k most frequent in North American child-directed speech (CHILDES). Irregular status assigned by hand.' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame({"top k verbs": m["k"], "irregular": m["irregular"], "share": np.array(m["irregular"]) / np.array(m["k"]), "k / ln k": np.array(m["k"]) / np.log(m["k"]), "share of verb tokens covered": m["token_share"]}).set_index("top k verbs").round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
irregular share k / ln k share of verb tokens covered
top k verbs
10 8 0.80 4.34 0.57

``` ::: ::: Irregular verbs are concentrated among frequent ones, so the irregular share falls steadily with vocabulary size. Under frequency-ordered learning the three thresholds predict onset near 120 verbs (majority), 310 (a 30% cutoff) and 800 ($N/\ln N$). These are far enough apart to tell which is right, **if a child's verb vocabulary at onset can be measured.** The same table shows why that is hard: the 200 most frequent verbs cover 96% of verb tokens, so everything beyond them shares 4%. ### Parent report Wordbank holds parent checklists for thousands of children. The English form lists 103 verbs, asks about 20 irregular past forms, and asks whether the child says each of 31 overregularized forms such as *blowed*. ::: {#cell-fig-wordbank .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} w = R["wordbank_english"] fig, ax = plt.subplots() ax.plot(w["verbs"], w["exception_share"], marker="o", ms=3, label="irregular share of known checklist verbs") ax.plot(w["verbs"][1:], 1 / np.log(w["verbs"][1:]), "k--", lw=1, label="1 / ln N on checklist counts") ax.plot(w["verbs"], w["any_overreg"], marker="s", ms=3, color="C3", label="children overregularizing") ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_xlabel("checklist verbs produced (of 103)"); ax.set_ylabel("proportion"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![English Wordbank. Left axis: share of the checklist verbs a child knows that are irregular. Right axis: share of children whose parent reports at least one overregularized verb form. Both by number of checklist verbs produced.](08-strategies_files/figure-html/fig-wordbank-output-1.png){#fig-wordbank} ::: ::: - **The checklist's irregular share is flat,** at about 46%, whatever the child's vocabulary. The checklist is a fixed sample of early, frequent verbs, 46 of which are irregular. On checklist counts no child ever comes near $N/\ln N$. - **Reported overregularization rises smoothly** with verb vocabulary, from under 10% of children to about three quarters. - **Everything turns on the verbs that are not on the list.** They are mostly regular, so the true irregular share is lower than the checklist's. How much lower depends on how many unlisted verbs the child knows. We tried to estimate that from input frequency: fit how a child's chance of knowing a checklist verb depends on its frequency, and apply the fit to all 1,385 verbs in the input. The estimate is not usable. ::: {#tbl-tail .cell tbl-cap='Estimated verb inventory of a child producing 90 checklist verbs, and the checklist count at which each threshold predicts onset, under four assumptions about unlisted verbs. \'None\' means not by 100 checklist verbs.' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} t = pd.DataFrame(R["tail_model"]).rename(columns={ "assumption": "assumption about unlisted verbs", "verbs_at_90": "total verbs", "irregular_at_90": "irregular", "onset_TP": "onset under N / ln N", "onset_30": "onset under 30% cutoff"}) t[["total verbs", "irregular"]] = t[["total verbs", "irregular"]].round(0) t.set_index("assumption about unlisted verbs") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
total verbs irregular onset under N / ln N onset under 30% cutoff
assumption about unlisted verbs
slope fitted to parent report 943.0 107.0 3.0 3
same, off-checklist verbs harder 645.0 90.0 80.0 3
slope fitted to children's production 495.0 90.0 96.0 57
steeper slope 339.0 83.0 NaN 80
``` ::: ::: The predicted onset under $N/\ln N$ runs from "immediately" to "never" depending on an assumption the data cannot check. Frequency predicts which verbs a child knows only weakly (the correlation across checklist verbs is about 0.3, in line with the wider literature on age of acquisition), and the checklist contains almost no rare verbs to calibrate on. ### Transcripts Transcripts record what a child actually says, so in principle the whole verb inventory is observable. CHILDES has 15 English-learning children with more than 50,000 words between 18 and 42 months. ::: {#tbl-dense .cell tbl-cap='The ten densest English child corpora in CHILDES, 18 to 42 months. Hours are missing where transcripts carry no media timestamps.' execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame(R["dense"]).rename(columns={"tokens": "child tokens", "hours": "hours recorded"}).set_index("corpus").round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The difficulty is that a sample of speech shows only the verbs used often enough to appear in it. Raw counts therefore depend on how much was recorded. ::: {#cell-fig-thinning .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} th = R["thinning"] fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 3.5)) ax[0].plot(th["tokens"], th["types_rel"], marker="o", ms=3, label="all verb types") ax[0].plot(th["tokens"], th["irregular_rel"], marker="s", ms=3, label="irregular types") ax[0].set_xscale("log"); ax[0].set_ylim(0, 1.05) ax[0].set_xlabel("verb tokens kept"); ax[0].set_ylabel("count, relative to the full sample"); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8) ax[1].plot(th["tokens"], th["irregular_share"], marker="o", ms=3, color="C3") ax[1].set_xscale("log"); ax[1].set_ylim(0, 0.6) ax[1].set_xlabel("verb tokens kept"); ax[1].set_ylabel("apparent irregular share") fig.tight_layout(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Raw counts are a function of sample size. For 12 densely recorded child-by-window samples, tokens were randomly removed and the verbs recounted. The same children appear to know fewer verbs, and a higher share of irregulars, the less of their speech is kept.](08-strategies_files/figure-html/fig-thinning-output-1.png){#fig-thinning} ::: ::: Rare verbs are the ones lost, and rare verbs are mostly regular, so a small sample inflates the irregular share. This is the bias @yang2016 invokes for the children who exceed the threshold, and it is large: the same children show an irregular share of about 54% in a hundred or so verb tokens and 28% in eight thousand. One might hope to correct for it. The following result suggests the problem is deeper. ::: {#cell-fig-rarefaction .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} r = R["rarefaction"] fig, ax = plt.subplots() ax.fill_between(r["age"], r["types_q25"], r["types_q75"], alpha=0.2) ax.plot(r["age"], r["types_median"], marker="o", ms=4, label="verb types") ax.plot(r["age"], r["irregular_median"], marker="s", ms=4, color="C3", label="irregular verb types") for a, y, n in zip(r["age"], r["types_median"], r["children"]): ax.text(a, y + 9, str(n), ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color="0.4") ax.set_ylim(0, 160); ax.set_xlabel("age at start of 3-month window (months)") ax.set_ylabel("types in 1,000 verb tokens"); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Distinct verbs in a fixed sample of 1,000 verb tokens, by age. Each child's speech in a three-month window was randomly reduced to 1,000 verb tokens. Line: median across children; band: interquartile range; numbers: children per window.](08-strategies_files/figure-html/fig-rarefaction-output-1.png){#fig-rarefaction} ::: ::: **At a fixed sample size, the number of distinct verbs is flat from 18 to 42 months,** at about 115, and so is the number of irregulars, at about 48. The make-up of the verbs by frequency band is flat as well. The apparent growth of verb vocabulary in transcripts is growth in how much children talk. The verbs learned between two and three years are mostly too rare to appear in a sample of this size. They are below its resolution, and no reweighting of the verbs that do appear can recover them without an outside assumption about how often a known verb is used. Two estimators we tried illustrate this. One that assumed children use each verb at its rate in the input credited a child with 1,200 verbs from 240 observed. One that modelled knowledge and usage jointly was stable under thinning but returned nearly the same vocabulary for every child at every age. A caveat: children with 1,000 verb tokens in three months at 18 months are unusually talkative, so the youngest windows are a selected group. The consequence for the developmental test of @sec-evidence is direct. Counts of $N$ and $e$ taken from transcripts at a child's first overregularization mostly measure how many tokens had been recorded by then. They can neither refute the principle nor confirm it. ### A second language Norwegian is a useful contrast, because it has no single regular past tense, and Wordbank has dense longitudinal data for it. ::: {#tbl-norwegian .cell tbl-cap='Norwegian past-tense classes on the parent checklist (classified by hand), and their share among the checklist verbs children know.' execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} nw = R["norwegian"] pd.DataFrame({"checklist verbs": nw["checklist"], "share among verbs known": nw["share_known"]}).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
checklist verbs share among verbs known
strong 40 0.38
weak -et/-a 38 0.35
weak -te 26 0.24
weak -de/-dde 3 0.03
``` ::: ::: No class is a majority. On checklist counts, the largest weak class has about 65% exceptions, so none of the thresholds considered licenses any suffix as a general past-tense rule. Children overregularize regardless: about three quarters of those near the checklist ceiling are reported to. ::: {#tbl-norwegian-pairs .cell tbl-cap='Norwegian: number of children reported to say each of two overregularized forms of the same strong verb.' execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} p = pd.DataFrame(nw["pairs"]).rename(columns={"et": "-et form", "n_et": "children (-et)", "te": "-te form", "n_te": "children (-te)"}) p.loc[len(p)] = ["total", p["children (-et)"].sum(), "total", p["children (-te)"].sum()] p ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
-et form children (-et) -te form children (-te)
0 drikket 976 drikte 1171
1 finnet 345 finte 349
2 fryset 218 fryste 706
3 hjelpet 557 hjelpte 1347
4 holdet 88 holdte 670
5 løpet 291 løpte 1188
6 sprekket 63 sprekte 193
7 synget 440 syngte 950
8 total 2978 total 6574
``` ::: ::: For the same verbs, children more often choose *-te*, the suffix of the smaller class. Some *-et* forms coincide with real participles, which should inflate reports of them, so the preference may be understated. A single threshold on type counts over the whole class cannot produce this pattern. The usual response is that each suffix is a rule over a phonologically defined sub-class and is evaluated there. That is plausible, but it means the domain of the rule has to be known before $N$ and $e$ can be counted, which is the analyst's freedom noted in @sec-evidence. ## A way to rescue the corpus route The missing ingredient is a measure of what a child knows that does not depend on sampling, taken on the same children as the recordings. Parent report is such a measure for the verbs on the checklist. With both in hand: 1. Take the checklist verbs as the parent reports them. 2. Among verbs the parent says the child knows, observe how often a known verb actually appears in a sample of a given size, as a function of its frequency. This measures the detection curve instead of assuming it. 3. Apply that curve to the verbs heard that are not on the checklist, counting each as one divided by its chance of being heard. In simulation, with the real verb list and frequencies, this recovers total verb vocabulary to within about 0 to 20% at the median from 500 to 8,000 verb tokens per child, where raw counts are 20 to 70% low. Two cautions apply. The simulated children follow the family of usage laws that the estimator fits, and they do not reproduce the flatness shown above, so real performance will be worse. And the method needs child speech that is correctly attributed to the child, which is not a given for automatically processed home recordings. ## Comparison | | Experiment | Parent report | Transcripts | Parent report + recordings | |---|---|---|---|---| | Range of $N$ | 9 to about 25 | tens to hundreds | tens to hundreds | tens to hundreds | | $N$ and $e$ known? | by design, if learning is checked | only for listed verbs | only for frequent verbs | estimated, with a measured detection curve | | Measure of productivity | generalization to new items | reported overregularization | observed overregularization | either | | Main obstacle | long sessions with children | verbs off the checklist | sample resolution | accurate attribution of child speech; few children | | Tests the functional form? | yes, with the reversal design | not without the tail | no | possibly | The experiment is the only route that tests the form directly, and it is expensive. The corpus route is cheap and covers the right range, but neither parent report nor transcripts alone identifies a child's verb vocabulary. Combining them is the most promising way to make the corpus route work.
